items.claim: Domain enumeration in Active Directory can be driven from PowerView loaded as a plain script, so a hunter does not need the RSAT/AD PowerShell modules installed on the host to map the domain.
items.body:
Domain enumeration in Active Directory can be driven from PowerView loaded as a plain script, so a hunter does not need the RSAT/AD PowerShell modules installed on the host to map the domain.

HackTricks reference: 152098c3 (notion:152098c3-95c5-80ff-938f-f6e8d8e51320)
items.disproof: PowerView fails to load or its domain queries return no objects, showing this path is not usable against the target.

items.claim: AD objects can be harvested straight over LDAP with a filter plus an explicit attribute list, so an in-memory .NET enumerator covers the same ground as PowerView and can pull specific attributes such as a group's cn and member set.

items.disproof: The LDAP search returns nothing or is refused, so the objects cannot be enumerated directly and a different channel is required.

sources.quote:
First import the module.

powershell-import C:\Tools\PowerSploit\Recon\PowerView.ps1

image.png

Getting information aboput current domain

powershell Get-Domain

image.png

Gitting infromation about Domain Controller

powershell Get-DomainController | select Forest, Name, OSVersion | fl

image.png

Enumerating the Forest

powershell Get-ForestDomain

image.png

Enumerating Group Policy

powershell Get-DomainPolicyData | select -expand SystemAccess

image.png

Enumerating Domain Users

powershell Get-DomainUser -Identity jking -Properties DisplayName, MemberOf | fl

image.png

Enumerationg Domain Computer

powershell Get-DomainComputer -Properties DnsHostName | sort -Property DnsHostName

image.png

Enumerating OU

powershell Get-DomainOU -Properties Name | sort -Property Name

image.png

Enumerating Groups

powershell Get-DomainGroup | where Name -like "*Admins*" | select SamAccountName

image.png

Enumerating Group Members

powershell Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" | select MemberDistinguishedName

image.png

Enumerating Group Policy Objects

powershell Get-DomainGPO -Properties DisplayName | sort -Property DisplayName

image.png

Enumerating Local GPOS

powershell Get-DomainGPOLocalGroup | select GPODisplayName, GroupName

image.png

Enumerating Machines where the user is member of a local group

powershell Get-DomainGPOUserLocalGroupMapping -LocalGroup Administrators | select ObjectName, GPODisplayName, ContainerName, ComputerName | fl

image.png

Enumerating Domain Trust.

powershell Get-DomainTrust

image.png

yellowhbSharpView

Same as PowerView.

execute-assembly C:\Tools\SharpView\SharpView\bin\Release\SharpView.exe Get-Domain

image.png

yellowhbADSearch

uses ldap queries to retrive information

execute-assembly C:\Tools\ADSearch\ADSearch\bin\Release\ADSearch.exe --search "objectCategory=user"

image.png

we can use filters

execute-assembly C:\Tools\ADSearch\ADSearch\bin\Release\ADSearch.exe --search "(&(objectCategory=group)(cn=*Admins))"

image.png

we can also specify the attributes that matches our interests.

execute-assembly C:\Tools\ADSearch\ADSearch\bin\Release\ADSearch.exe --search "(&(objectCategory=group)(cn=MS SQL Admins))" --attributes cn,member

image.png

In summary, a filter is evaluated to "TRUE", "FALSE", or "Undefined". If the filter evaluates to TRUE for a particular entry, then the attributes of that entry are returned as part of the Search result (subject to any applicable access control restrictions).
